newsitem.title: CHINA: Cambodia's king denies endorsing new government.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's king denies endorsing new government.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk denied on Thursday that he endorsed Phnom Penh's new government during a meeting in Beijing with newly appointed First Prime Minister Ung Huot.

"It is not true that I have given my blessing to the new 'team' of his excellency Hun Sen (and) in particular to his excellency Ung Huot," Sihanouk said in a letter to his son, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who was toppled by strongman Hun Sen last month.
A copy of the letter was sent to reporters in Beijing, where the king has been receiving medical treatment since February.
"I never gave him the title of first prime minister which, in full legality, still belongs to you," Sihanouk told his son.
Hun Sen ousted Sihanouk's son on July 6 and then backed Ung Huot's nomination to replace him.

Hun Sen and Ung Huot had travelled to Beijing to seek the king's blessing -- a move political analysts in Phnom Penh said was the last hurdle facing Hun Sen in his bid to legitimise his new government.

Ung Huot told reporters on his return to Phnom Penh from Beijing earlier that Sihanouk had given his blessing to Cambodia's new government during five hours of talks at the king residence in the Chinese capital on Tuesday.
Sihanouk denied this. "During the audience and the lunch on August 12, 1997, I never gave my 'blessing' to these Cambodian 'guests'," he said.
"At the above mentioned lunch, I only raised my glass, saying to them 'To your health'. This conformed to our tradition."
Last week Sihanouk called Ung Huot a "puppet" of Hun Sen and said he still recognised Ranariddh as the legitimate first prime minister.
Hun Sen had previously ruled with Ranariddh in an uneasy coalition government that took power after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Sihanouk had offered on Monday to abdicate but said later that Hun Sen refused the offer during their Tuesday meeting.

The king said on Thursday he would return to Cambodia before the end of the month to hold a Buddhist ceremony for peace and national reconciliation in Siem Reap, home of the famed Angkor temple complex.
Hun Sen told reporters in Phnom Penh that he had assured Sihanouk that he was the defender of the monarchy.
"I told the king and queen, please consider us the defenders of the monarchy. If anyone wants to end the monarchy, they have to put an end to my life first," he said.

Hun Sen dismissed a suggestion from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) that an informal meeting of all parties involved in the Cambodian problem, including Ranariddh and Hun Sen, should be held.
ASEAN postponed Cambodia's entry to the group after Ranariddh was overthrown and has been trying to mediate a solution to the country's problems.
Hun Sen insisted that if Ranariddh returned to Cambodia he would have to face charges for illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.
The Cambodian National Assembly voted last week to strip Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity and a military court subsequently issued a warrant for his arrest.
Asked if Ranariddh would be allowed to take part in an election planned for May next year, Hun Sen said: "The question of joining the election or not, you have to ask the court."
